headline: High: shared file-based workflows and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error risks; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A ingests PDFs, text, images, and draw.io XML and uses MCP/browser tooling; Agent B reads/writes files and runs shell in a local dev environment. A shared workspace or copied artifacts would let B parse A-produced content as instructions. No direct bridge is documented, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF Agent B consumes files exported by Agent A without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace directory, attacker-controlled document content can cross the boundary.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Disable automatic execution of instructions found in documents.
Add provenance labels to exported files.
Review any MCP tool calls before execution.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and allowlist parsing for imported diagrams/text.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A handles API keys and can use broad network egress; Agent B handles configuration secrets and has filesystem read/write plus allowlisted egress. If they share files or environment material, secrets or sensitive documents can flow from one agent to the other and out through network calls. The pairwise leak path is plausible in default local-development setups.
conditions: IF a shared directory contains secrets or sensitive documents, the other agent can read them.
IF either agent forwards file contents to external APIs, those contents may leave the local environment.
mitigations: Store secrets in separate per-agent env files.
Mount read-only inputs for one-way transfers.
Rotate any exposed API keys.
Restrict outbound domains to the minimum needed.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent secret isolation in the orchestrator.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent A supports multiple instances and MCP/browser-driven document processing; Agent B supports multiple instances, shell, subprocesses, and filesystem writes. Even without git writes, concurrent writes to shared files or generated artifacts can race and corrupt outputs. The profiles do not state locking or isolation, so the conflict is plausible in default local runs.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same output directory, file clobbering can occur.
IF Agent A and Agent B run concurrently against shared artifacts, race conditions can corrupt generated work products.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories.
Run one agent at a time for shared artifacts.
Use file locks for any shared writes.
Make outputs append-only where possible.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking and namespace isolation.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A produces AI-assisted visualizations and document transformations; Agent B is an agentic RAG/content-writing system with API endpoints and shell execution. If B treats A's generated diagrams or extracted text as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream writes or actions. Because B has action-taking capability and no verification step is documented, the blast radius is high.
conditions: IF Agent B uses Agent A outputs as source-of-truth without verification, incorrect facts can propagate.
IF Agent B triggers shell or API actions from A-generated content, downstream mistakes can become operational.
mitigations: Require human review before B acts on A outputs.
Add a verification step against original sources.
Mark A outputs as untrusted by default.
Log provenance for every transformed artifact.
requires-engineering: implement confidence-gated action execution in B.

E_compliance.rationale: Agent A handles API keys and document content; Agent B handles academic papers plus configuration secrets and runs in a local development environment with third-party APIs. The profiles do not document residency, retention, or DPA alignment, so a compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. Because both are open-source and the mismatch is indirect, medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into either agent, retention and residency obligations must be checked.
IF Agent B sends paper or secret content to external APIs, policy mismatches may occur.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in both agents.
Review API vendor data-processing terms.
Set explicit retention limits where configurable.
Document which data classes each agent may process.
requires-engineering: add residency and retention controls to the deployment.
